title: Prairieland ICE detention-center attack
claim: An organized Antifa cell used firearms, explosives, and coordinated tactics against an ICE facility and responding police.
evidence: A federal jury convicted nine defendants in March 2026. Prosecutors introduced encrypted planning messages, ideological materials, weapons, fireworks, and evidence that an officer was shot in an ambush.
attribution: This is the strongest recent U.S. evidence for a self-consciously Antifa-aligned cell committing organized political violence. The convictions support the cell-level attribution; they do not by themselves prove a national organization.

title: Killing of Aaron Danielson in Portland
claim: A self-described Antifa supporter killed a right-wing protest participant.
evidence: Police obtained an arrest warrant for Michael Reinoehl in Danielson’s shooting. Reinoehl called himself “100% ANTIFA” and claimed self-defense in an interview; federal officers killed him before the case could be tried.

title: Violence during Portland’s 2020 protests
claim: Antifa was responsible for the Portland disorder.
evidence: Militant antifascists were present and some participants engaged in arson, vandalism, assaults, and repeated confrontations at the federal courthouse. Many other protesters were unaffiliated and peaceful, and criminal cases generally charged individual conduct rather than membership.
attribution: Specific acts can be attributed when evidence identifies an offender and motive. “Antifa caused Portland” is too broad: it converts a heterogeneous protest wave and months of separate events into one actor.
scope: Mixed movement, event, and individual conduct

title: Direct Action Minnesota indictment
claim: A Minneapolis direct-action group with Antifa ties ran a coordinated harassment and violence campaign against law enforcement.
evidence: A federal indictment charges 15 people with conspiracy, threats, stalking, assault, and property destruction. Fourteen defendants pleaded not guilty on July 1; Kyle Wagner separately pleaded not guilty after his transfer. DOJ alleges that the defendants included members of Antifa groups.
attribution: The indictment is meaningful evidence of alleged local organization, but the pleas preserve every contested element for trial. The precise nature of the claimed Antifa ties must be tested against the evidence rather than inferred from protest participation.

title: Kyle Wagner threat and cyberstalking case
claim: A self-identified Antifa member threatened immigration officers and doxxed a pro-ICE individual.
evidence: A federal grand jury indicted Wagner for cyberstalking and interstate threats, and a separate Minnesota indictment includes conspiracy and solicitation allegations. He pleaded not guilty. In August, the Sixth Circuit reversed a release order and kept him detained pending trial.
attribution: Wagner’s self-identification makes the individual ideological attribution relevant, but an indictment and detention ruling do not prove guilt. The public record does not establish direction by a broader Antifa command.

title: Antifa Ost in Germany
claim: A named European Antifa group organized cross-border assaults on perceived far-right targets.
evidence: German and Hungarian cases, U.S. intelligence reporting, and prosecutions identify a discrete militant network whose members allegedly planned and carried out coordinated attacks.
attribution: Unlike the U.S. umbrella movement, Antifa Ost is a specific named network. Its existence cannot be generalized into proof that every group using “antifa” belongs to one international organization.
